screens.title: 2D Physics & Collisions
screens.subtitle: Make objects move, collide, and detect overlaps with Rigidbody2D and Collider2D

narration.text: In this chapter you'll learn how Unity models 2D motion and contact using two core components: Rigidbody2D, which gives an object physical behavior, and Collider2D, which defines the object's collision shape. We'll look at body types — Dynamic, Kinematic, and Static — and when to use each. You'll also learn about collider families: box, circle, polygon, and edge; how physics materials control friction and bounciness; and how to respond in code with OnCollisionEnter2D and OnTriggerEnter2D. A concrete example will guide you: building a simple platformer where the player falls under gravity, lands on ground colliders, and picks up coins with trigger colliders. Along the way we'll point out common mistakes, like moving a Rigidbody by changing transform. position or forgetting that at least one object needs a Rigidbody2D for collisions to register. By the end you'll be able to choose efficient collider types, apply physics materials for desired surface behavior, and implement robust collision and trigger handling. Think of this chapter as the practical foundation for believable 2D interactions in your games.

keyIdea.title: Core Idea
keyIdea.text: Rigidbody2D provides physics behavior; Collider2D defines collision shape. Use body type and collider choice to balance accuracy and performance.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify and configure Rigidbody2D and Collider2D components correctly, choose the right collider type for common sprites, set up Physics Material 2D properties to shape surface behavior, and write code that responds to collisions and triggers. For example, you'll add a Rigidbody2D to a player, freeze its rotation to avoid unwanted spinning, and use a BoxCollider2D sized slightly smaller than the sprite so jumps feel forgiving. You'll also be able to explain the difference between OnCollisionEnter2D and OnTriggerEnter2D, why at least one Rigidbody2D is required for collision events, and how to avoid the common mistake of moving physics objects by setting transform. position instead of using Rigidbody2D velocity or MovePosition within FixedUpdate. These skills let you create playable platformers, collectible pickups, and performant level collision layers. You'll practice a hands-on activity that creates a ground, a dynamic player, and a trigger coin, then test detection and debug issues like missed triggers or jittery motion.

screens.title: Rigidbody2D: What it is and why it matters
screens.subtitle: Make a GameObject subject to 2D physics

narration.text: A Rigidbody2D is the component that makes a GameObject participate in Unity's 2D physics system. It tells Unity to compute velocity, acceleration, respond to gravity and forces, and handle collisions. In practice, you add a Rigidbody2D to any object that should move naturally, be pushed, or trigger collision callbacks. Key properties include Body Type (Dynamic, Kinematic, Static), Mass, Linear Drag, and Gravity Scale. Dynamic bodies are affected by forces and collisions and are used for players and moveable objects. Kinematic bodies are driven by scripts; they are useful for moving platforms or doors you animate by setting position in FixedUpdate or using MovePosition. Static bodies never move and are the most efficient for walls and ground. A common error is omitting Rigidbody2D and expecting collisions to fire — colliders alone don't trigger physics responses. Another pitfall is moving a Rigidbody by changing transform. position every frame; that bypasses the physics solver and causes jitter. Use Rigidbody2D. velocity, AddForce, or MovePosition from FixedUpdate so physics stays stable. For example, for a player character set Gravity Scale to tune fall speed and Freeze Rotation Z to prevent spinning when colliding. Reflect: which body type best fits an object you want to script-move but not have gravity affect?

keyIdea.title: Rigidbody2D
keyIdea.text: Adds physical behavior: body type selection determines how the object responds to forces and collisions.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Rigidbody2D
Rigidbody2D overview
Gives objects physical properties like mass, gravity, and velocity.
Body Types
  • Dynamic: affected by forces and collisions — use for players and movable objects.
  • Kinematic: moved by script, not by forces — use for moving platforms.
  • Static: immovable, best for ground and walls.
Important properties
Mass, Linear Drag, Gravity Scale and Constraints (freeze rotation Z to prevent spin).
Common mistake
Moving a Rigidbody by setting transform.position causes jitter and breaks the physics solver. Use Rigidbody2D velocity, AddForce, or MovePosition in FixedUpdate instead.
Concrete example
Player object: add Rigidbody2D, set Body Type to Dynamic, set Gravity Scale to 3 for snappier falls, and freeze Z rotation. Use BoxCollider2D sized slightly smaller than sprite for forgiving collisions.
Key Takeaway

Rigidbody2D enables realistic motion and collision callbacks; choose body type to match intended behavior and update physics properties in FixedUpdate.

Try this
Add Rigidbody2D to your player and increase Gravity Scale from 1 to 3. Observe fall speed change.
Check
If the player spins on impact, enable Freeze Rotation Z in Constraints.

screens.title: Collider2D: Shapes that define contact
screens.subtitle: Colliders define where and how objects collide without moving them

narration.text: A Collider2D defines the physical outline of an object for collision and trigger events. Unlike a Rigidbody2D, a collider does not impart movement; it only establishes the boundaries that other objects can contact. Common collider types pull from this idea: BoxCollider2D for rectangular objects, CircleCollider2D for round items, PolygonCollider2D for complex outlines, and EdgeCollider2D for open chains of lines. Colliders should generally be slightly smaller than the visible sprite to make collisions feel fair and avoid snagging. Performance matters: simple shapes like boxes and circles are much less expensive than polygons, so prefer them when they match your sprite. When editing a collider in the Scene view, you can tweak size and offset; make iterative adjustments while running the scene to confirm feel. Remember that colliders alone won't cause collision callbacks; at least one of the interacting objects must have a Rigidbody2D attached. A frequent misconception is that more precise colliders always improve gameplay — often a simpler collider yields better performance and a more predictable experience. Try sizing your character's collider slightly inside the sprite to see how it reduces accidental collisions.

keyIdea.title: Collider2D
keyIdea.text: Defines collision boundaries. Prefer simple shapes for performance; tweak size for fair gameplay.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Collider2D
Collider types and behavior
Define where physics interactions happen; edit size and offset to polish gameplay.
BoxCollider2D
Efficient for platforms, walls, and blocky sprites.
CircleCollider2D
Great for rolling or round objects; cheap and smooth for collisions.
PolygonCollider2D
Fits complex outlines precisely but costs more CPU. Use only when needed.
EdgeCollider2D
Series of connected lines useful for terrains and one-sided collisions.
Practical tip
Make colliders slightly smaller than the sprite to reduce frustrating catches on corners. Test in play mode and adjust offsets as needed.
Key Takeaway

Choose the simplest collider that matches shape. Precision costs CPU; player experience often improves with slightly forgiving shapes.

Try this
Swap a PolygonCollider2D to a BoxCollider2D for a static crate sprite and observe CPU cost and collision feel.

screens.title: Box vs Circle vs Polygon vs Edge
screens.subtitle: When to choose each Collider2D type

narration.text: Selecting the right Collider2D type involves balancing shape fidelity and performance. BoxCollider2D and CircleCollider2D are computationally efficient and should be your first choice whenever they match the sprite. Boxes are ideal for platforms, crates, tile-based objects and characters that approximate a rectangle. Circles are excellent for round projectiles, coins, and rolling objects where smooth rotation matters. PolygonCollider2D fits complex sprite outlines precisely, which is useful for detailed irregular objects, but it increases collision vertex counts and C P U work. Use polygons only when the extra precision materially affects gameplay. EdgeCollider2D defines a chain of lines; it's perfect for ground terrain or levels where you only need one-sided collisions and don't require a closed volume. A concrete case: a mountain skyline works well with an EdgeCollider2D because the player should land on the top surface without colliding from below. Remember the general rule: prefer simple shapes for performance and switch to polygons only when collisions require the shape's precision. Also, always profile if you suspect collider complexity is affecting framerate. Box vs Circle vs Polygon vs Edge means prefer box and circle colliders for performance; reserve polygon colliders for necessary precision and use edge colliders for terrain lines.. In practical terms, when to choose each collider2d type. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Collider Choice
keyIdea.text: Prefer box and circle colliders for performance; reserve polygon colliders for necessary precision and use edge colliders for terrain lines.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Collider Comparison
Collider Comparison
Quick guidance and a one-line use case for each collider type.
BoxCollider2D
Use for platforms, walls, crates. Fast and stable.
CircleCollider2D
Use for coins, round enemies, rolling objects. Smooth collisions.
PolygonCollider2D
Use for irregular sprites where precise outline matters; expensive.
EdgeCollider2D
Use for terrain lines or one-sided collision surfaces.
Example
Replace a PolygonCollider2D on a tileable floor with an EdgeCollider2D chain for better performance and simpler collision behavior when only the top surface matters.
Pitfall
Using PolygonCollider2D for many small decorative objects will increase CPU and memory usage unnecessarily.
Key Takeaway

Match collider complexity to gameplay need: start simple and move to precise shapes only when collision accuracy affects play.

screens.title: Physics Material 2D
screens.subtitle: Control friction and bounciness between surfaces

narration.text: Physics Material 2D assets let you specify how surfaces interact during collisions. The two primary properties are Friction, which resists sliding motion between contacting surfaces, and Bounciness, which determines how much kinetic energy is retained and returned after a collision. To create one, right-click in the Project window and choose Create > 2D > Physics Material 2D, then assign it to a Collider2D in the Inspector. Use low friction for ice-like surfaces where the player should slide, and high bounciness for trampoline-like platforms. A concrete example: create a platform material with high bounciness and apply it to a moving platform to give the player a springy rebound. Remember that physics materials combine: the effective friction during contact is based on properties of both colliders, so test interactions jointly. Overuse of extreme bounciness can produce uncontrollable behavior; tune values incrementally. Also keep in mind performance is not significantly affected by materials, but physics stability can be — very high bounciness combined with improper mass values may cause jitter. The safe strategy is small iterative changes with play-mode testing. Physics Material 2D means set friction and bounciness to craft sliding or bouncing behavior; test combinations for stable gameplay.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Physics Material 2D
Physics Material 2D
Paint surface behavior using friction and bounciness.
Friction
Controls sliding resistance. Low values create slippery surfaces; high values prevent sliding.
Bounciness
Controls rebound energy. Values near 1 keep energy; near 0 absorb energy.
Creation & application
Create a Physics Material 2D asset in the Project window and assign it to any Collider2D component in the Inspector.
Example
Create a bouncy platform material and apply it to a platform to see the player rebound on landing.
Warning
High bounciness with low mass can cause unstable behavior. Tune mass and bounciness together.
Key Takeaway

Materials let you craft sliding and springy surfaces. Adjust gradually and test interactions between colliders.

screens.title: Collision callbacks: OnCollisionEnter2D
screens.subtitle: Respond to physical contacts in code

narration.text: When two non-trigger Collider2D objects meet and at least one has a Rigidbody2D, Unity calls collision callbacks such as OnCollisionEnter2D, OnCollisionStay2D, and OnCollisionExit2D. These methods receive a Collision2D object that contains contact information and a reference to the other GameObject. Use OnCollisionEnter2D to detect landing on ground or hitting an enemy and inspect collision. gameObject to check tags or components. For example, a player script can check if the collided object has the tag Ground and then set an isGrounded flag. Note that collision callbacks deliver physics contact points, so you can examine collision. contacts if you need the exact collision normal for effects. A common misconception is that triggers and collisions behave the same; collisions produce physical response and are meant for blocking and reaction, while triggers only detect overlap without physical resolution. Also ensure collision events will fire by verifying layer collision matrix settings and that at least one collider has a Rigidbody2D. Use these callbacks for landing detection, bounce logic, or damage application on impact. Collision callbacks: OnCollisionEnter2D means used for physical contacts; receives collision2d with info about the contact and other gameobject.. In practical terms, respond to physical contacts in code. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: OnCollisionEnter2D
keyIdea.text: Used for physical contacts; receives Collision2D with info about the contact and other GameObject.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › OnCollisionEnter2D
Collision callbacks
Use these for physical responses like landing, bouncing, or taking damage on impact.
  • OnCollisionEnter2D fires on contact start.
  • OnCollisionStay2D while contact persists.
  • OnCollisionExit2D when contact ends.
Key Takeaway

Collisions are for physical interaction. Use the Collision2D data to inspect contact points and the other GameObject.

Example script snippet
// OnCollisionEnter2D example
void OnCollisionEnter2D(Collision2D collision)
{
  Debug.Log("Collided with: " + collision.gameObject.name);
  if (collision.gameObject.CompareTag("Ground"))
  {
    Debug.Log("Player landed on ground!");
  }
}
Use collision.gameObject to check tags or components. Inspect collision.contacts for normals if you need directional responses.
Misconception
Collision callbacks will not fire if both colliders are static or if layer settings prevent the collision. Ensure at least one Rigidbody2D exists.

narration.text: Triggers let you detect overlaps between colliders without producing a physical response. To use them, check the "Is Trigger" box on a Collider2D. When a trigger overlap occurs and at least one object in the pair has a Rigidbody2D, Unity calls OnTriggerEnter2D, OnTriggerStay2D and OnTriggerExit2D. Triggers are ideal for pickups, entry zones, or detecting when an object enters a region. The typical pattern is to tag the collectible with "Coin" and implement OnTriggerEnter2D on the player to Destroy the coin when collected. Be careful: if both colliders are static triggers with no Rigidbody2D, no events will fire. Also remember triggers do not prevent objects from passing through each other; they only notify. A common pitfall is using triggers where a physical response is desired — for bounce or blocking behavior, use non-trigger colliders and collision callbacks instead. Finally, triggers are useful for optimization: a non-physical sensor can detect nearby items without creating complicated collision geometry. Triggers: OnTriggerEnter2D and friends means triggers detect overlap without physical collision; require at least one rigidbody2d to fire events.. In practical terms, detect overlaps without physics resolution. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Triggers
keyIdea.text: Triggers detect overlap without physical collision; require at least one Rigidbody2D to fire events.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Triggers
Trigger detection
Use triggers to detect overlaps like pickups and zones without physical blocking.
  • Enable "Is Trigger" on a Collider2D to make it a sensor.
  • OnTriggerEnter2D is called when overlap begins; OnTriggerExit2D when it ends.
  • At least one collider must have a Rigidbody2D for events to fire.
Key Takeaway

Triggers are detection-only and do not produce physical responses; use them for pickups and sensors.

Example script
// OnTriggerEnter2D example
void OnTriggerEnter2D(Collider2D other)
{
  Debug.Log("Triggered by: " + other.gameObject.name);
  if (other.gameObject.CompareTag("Coin"))
  {
    Debug.Log("Coin collected!");
    Destroy(other.gameObject);
  }
}
Attach this to the player. Ensure the coin has Is Trigger checked and that either coin or player has a Rigidbody2D.
Pitfall
If no Rigidbody2D is present on either object, trigger events will not fire. Add a Rigidbody2D to at least one object.

screens.title: Who needs a Rigidbody2D?
screens.subtitle: Rules for collision and trigger event delivery

narration.text: Understanding which objects need a Rigidbody2D is critical to ensure collisions and triggers fire. The rule of thumb is: at least one of the two interacting colliders must have a Rigidbody2D for Unity to compute physics contact and invoke callbacks. If both objects only have Collider2D components and no rigidbodies, they act as static colliders that do not produce collision events. If one object has a Rigidbody2D and another only has a Collider2D, collisions and triggers will work — this is common for players hitting static ground. If both objects have Rigidbody2D, they will both be simulated and respond to forces and impulses. For triggers, the same rule applies: Is Trigger only turns off physical resolution; the presence of a Rigidbody2D is still required for events to be dispatched. Also consider body types: a Kinematic Rigidbody2D interacts with Dynamic bodies and can be moved via script without being driven by physics forces. Use Static bodies for immovable level geometry to save C P U time. A practical debugging step is to temporarily add a Rigidbody2D to the static object to confirm whether missing events are due to lack of a rigidbody or layer collision settings.

keyIdea.title: Rigidbody Requirement
keyIdea.text: At least one object needs a Rigidbody2D for collisions and triggers to be detected and reported.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Rigidbody Rules
Which objects need a Rigidbody2D?
The presence of a Rigidbody2D determines whether Unity treats colliders as dynamic or static for events.
Both static colliders
No Rigidbody2D on either -> no collision callbacks; objects just overlap visually.
One with Rigidbody2D
Callbacks fire; common for player vs ground.
Both with Rigidbody2D
Both simulated; collisions cause physical response on both bodies.
If you see missing events, check the Rigidbody presence and the layer collision matrix in Project Settings > Physics 2D. Temporarily adding a Rigidbody2D to the suspected static object is a fast way to isolate the issue.
Debugging Tip

Add Rigidbody2D temporarily or toggle layer collisions to verify why an expected event didn't fire.

screens.title: Hands-on activity: Build basic platformer physics
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step editor and script setup

narration.text: This hands-on activity walks you through creating a ground, player, and coin as a simple platformer physics test. Step one: create a Ground GameObject, add BoxCollider2D and optionally a Sprite Renderer for visibility. Tag it as "Ground" if you plan to check for ground in scripts. Step two: add a Rigidbody2D to your Player object, set Body Type to Dynamic, set Gravity Scale to around 3 for a snappier fall, add a BoxCollider2D sized to the character, and freeze Z rotation in Constraints. Step three: create a Coin object with a CircleCollider2D, check Is Trigger, and either add a Kinematic Rigidbody2D or ensure the player has a Rigidbody2D so trigger events fire. Step four: write a small PlayerController2D script with an OnTriggerEnter2D method that checks CompareTag("Coin") and Destroy(other. gameObject) to collect it. Run the scene and verify the player falls onto the ground and collects coins. If physics looks jittery, confirm you are not moving the Rigidbody via transform in Update; instead, plan to use velocity or MovePosition in FixedUpdate. This activity consolidates the concepts and makes debugging patterns familiar.

keyIdea.text: Create ground, add Rigidbody2D to player, make coin a trigger, and implement OnTriggerEnter2D to collect coins.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Platformer Activity
Activity steps
Follow these editor actions and test in Play mode.
1) Create Ground
Empty GameObject → BoxCollider2D → optional Sprite Renderer. Tag as Ground.
2) Player setup
Add Rigidbody2D (Dynamic), Gravity Scale=3, BoxCollider2D, Freeze Rotation Z.

using UnityEngine;

public class PlayerController2D : MonoBehaviour
{
    void OnTriggerEnter2D(Collider2D other)
    {
        if (other.CompareTag("Coin"))

            Debug.Log("Coin collected!");
            Destroy(other.gameObject);
        }
    }
}
Attach this script to the Player. Run and verify coins disappear and console logs appear when collecting.
Debugging hint

If the coin doesn't trigger, confirm layer collisions and that at least one object has a Rigidbody2D. Also check tags match exactly.

screens.title: Common pitfalls and performance tips
screens.subtitle: Avoid jitter, missing callbacks, and expensive colliders

narration.text: Working with 2D physics often surfaces a handful of recurring issues. First, jitter and teleporting usually come from moving Rigidbody2D objects by setting transform. position in Update. The physics engine and transform updates can conflict, so move physics objects with Rigidbody2D. velocity, AddForce, or MovePosition in FixedUpdate. Second, missing events commonly result from both colliders being static or incorrect layer collision settings; always confirm at least one Rigidbody2D is present and inspect the Physics 2D layer collision matrix. Third, overlapping colliders at scene start can cause large separation forces as the solver resolves interpenetration; ensure objects are placed with clear initial spacing. Fourth, performance can degrade from many PolygonCollider2D instances or unnecessary Rigidbody2D on decorative objects; prefer Box or Circle colliders for large numbers of objects and leave static decorations without Rigidbody2D. Finally, extreme material bounciness combined with mismatched mass can cause unpredictable motion; tune mass, friction, and bounciness together and test iteratively. These practices help keep your physics stable and performant while delivering the intended gameplay experience. Common pitfalls and performance tips means move rigidbodies via physics apis, ensure rigidbody presence for events, and prefer simple colliders for performance.. In practical terms, avoid jitter, missing callbacks, and expensive colliders. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pitfalls & Tips
keyIdea.text: Move Rigidbodies via physics APIs, ensure Rigidbody presence for events, and prefer simple colliders for performance.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Troubleshooting
Common issues and fixes
A checklist to diagnose jitter, missing callbacks, and performance problems.
Jittery movement
Do not set transform.position every frame. Use Rigidbody2D.velocity, AddForce, or MovePosition in FixedUpdate.
Missing events
Ensure at least one object has Rigidbody2D and verify the Physics 2D layer collision matrix.
Startup overlap
Place objects without overlap to avoid solver pushing them apart violently at scene start.
Performance
Avoid many PolygonCollider2D instances; prefer simple shapes and static bodies where possible.
Key Takeaway

Use physics-aware movement, check layer rules and Rigidbody presence, and prefer simple colliders to keep your game stable and fast.

screens.title: Physics update timing: FixedUpdate and solver stability
screens.subtitle: Update physics at fixed intervals for deterministic behavior

narration.text: Unity separates rendering updates from physics updates. Physics calculations run on a fixed timestep and invoke FixedUpdate accordingly. If you apply forces or set Rigidbody2D velocities, do so inside FixedUpdate so those changes are applied in sync with the physics solver. Applying physics changes in Update can produce inconsistent forces between frames, causing slight differences that add up to jitter. For kinematic objects you move by script, use Rigidbody2D. MovePosition within FixedUpdate for the smoothest interaction with the solver. Also, be mindful of the fixed timestep value in Project Settings; reducing it increases physics frequency and C P U cost. A practical example: when applying gravity-like acceleration via code, add to velocity in FixedUpdate rather than Update. A common misconception is that Update is always fine because it runs every frame — physics expects fixed steps, and matching your physics code to that rhythm reduces non-deterministic behavior and makes collisions more reliable across hardware. After adjusting your code, test in both editor and target platforms to confirm stable behavior. Physics update timing: FixedUpdate and solver stability means apply physics updates inside fixedupdate; use moveposition for kinematic movement to keep the physics solver stable.. In practical terms, update physics at fixed intervals for deterministic behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: FixedUpdate
keyIdea.text: Apply physics updates inside FixedUpdate; use MovePosition for kinematic movement to keep the physics solver stable.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › FixedUpdate
Physics timing and stability
Make physics changes in FixedUpdate to match the solver's timestep.
Why FixedUpdate?
Physics runs at fixed intervals; applying forces there keeps behavior deterministic and reduces jitter.
Kinematic movement

Best practice

narration.text: These are the essential ideas to carry forward. Rigidbody2D makes objects part of the physics simulation; its Body Type determines whether the object is dynamic, kinematic, or static. Collider2D shapes define collision boundaries — choose box or circle when possible for performance, and use polygon or edge colliders only when necessary. Physics Material 2D controls friction and bounciness and should be tuned together with mass for stable results. Collision callbacks like OnCollisionEnter2D report physical contact, while trigger callbacks like OnTriggerEnter2D detect overlaps without physical resolution. Always ensure at least one interacting object has a Rigidbody2D and perform physics updates in FixedUpdate to keep behavior stable.
